native_result.query: In which domain do the majority of authors tend to be male for both original and replication studies?
native_result.HypoA: In Experimental Economics, the majority of authors tend to be male for both original and replication studies with ratio of males in original and replication studies being and 0.87 and 0.84 respectively.
native_result.HypoB: Economics is the only domain in the meta-regression heterogeneity data where the majority of authors tend to be male in both the original (mean authors_male.o = 0.870, median 1.000) and the replication (mean authors_male.r = 0.837, median 1.000); 55.6% (resp. 83.3%) of its 18 O/R pairs have a strict (resp. non-strict) male majority in BOTH the original and the replication, vs the two psychology disciplines (Cognitive mean_r=0.514, Social mean_r=0.504) which hover at parity in replications.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1. Loaded the study-level heterogeneity CSV (927 rows); confirmed discipline/authors_male.* columns and dtypes. 2. Verified that the 26 aggregated == True rows are exact re-aggregations of 26 aggregated == False rows (id overlap = 26/26); dropped those to avoid double counting, keeping both aggregated == False (786) and aggregated == NaN (115) for a primary slice of n = 901 (Cognitive 234, Economics 18, Social 649). 3. Per discipline, computed simple mean and median of authors_male.o and authors_male.r, an author-count-weighted mean (Σ n_authors · authors_male / Σ n_authors), and the share of O/R pairs in which BOTH originals and replications exceed 0.5 (and >= 0.5). 4. Ran two sensitivity slices: aggregated in {False, True} (n = 812, excludes Economics by construction because its aggregated flag is NaN) and the full 927-row set; the discipline ranking — Economics >> Cognitive ≈ Social — is invariant. 5. Wrote numeric outputs to artifacts/numbers.json and a Markdown summary to artifacts/summary.md.

sub_hypo.context: Original and replication studies in Experimental Economics.
sub_hypo.relations: Male authors constitute a majority in both original and replication studies: the male author ratio is 0.87 in original studies and 0.84 in replication studies.

gold_sub_hypo.full_hypo: In Experimental Economics, the majority of authors tend to be male for both original and replication studies with ratio of males in original and replication studies being and 0.87 and 0.84 respectively.

sub_hypo.text: Economics is the only discipline with predominantly male authors in both original and replication studies: the original male-author ratio has mean 0.870 and median 1.000, and the replication ratio has mean 0.837 and median 1.000. Cognitive and Social replications hover at gender parity, with mean male-author ratios of 0.514 and 0.504, respectively.
sub_hypo.context: Study-level meta-regression heterogeneity data, excluding 26 aggregated == True duplicate re-aggregations and retaining aggregated == False or missing: 901 original/replication pairs (234 Cognitive, 18 Economics, 649 Social).
sub_hypo.relations: Male-author ratios are higher in Economics in both original and replication studies; replication means follow Economics (0.837) > Cognitive (0.514) ≈ Social (0.504). Economics has an all-male median author composition in both study stages, whereas psychology replication means are near 0.5.

sub_hypo.text: Among the 18 Economics original/replication pairs, 55.6% have a strict male majority in both studies and 83.3% have a non-strict male majority in both studies.
sub_hypo.context: Economics pairs in the deduplicated 901-row primary heterogeneity-data slice, retaining aggregated == False or missing and excluding aggregated == True.
sub_hypo.relations: For Economics, 55.6% of pairs satisfy authors_male.o > 0.5 AND authors_male.r > 0.5; 83.3% satisfy authors_male.o >= 0.5 AND authors_male.r >= 0.5.
